newsitem.title: SPAIN: Spain backs full role in NATO, France holds out. [CORRECTED 18:35 GMT]
newsitem.headline: Spain backs full role in NATO, France holds out. [CORRECTED 18:35 GMT]

text.p: Parliament endorsed Spain's full integration in NATO's military command on Thursday, ending decades of ambivalence toward the Western alliance.
Prime Minister Jose Maria Aznar had urged closer links with NATO, saying circumstances have changed dramatically in recent years with the end of the Cold War and changes in the alliance.
NATO Secretary General Javier Solana, a former Spanish foreign minister (Corrects from defence minister), applauded the move.
"Spain's participation in the new structure will enable her to play her full part in reshaping the alliance to meet the challenges of tomorrow," Solana said in a statement.
Full integration means Spain will have a greater say in decisions made by NATO's military committee and a bigger presence in the command structure.
The Congress of Deputies or parliament voted 293-23 in favour of full integration with four abstentions.
"It is something to be pleased about, that such an important decision for the present and future of Spain has received such considerable (support)," said Defence Minister Eduardo Serra.

France, which pulled out of NATO's integrated command structure in the 1960s, said Spain's move would not deter it from a drive to entrust the alliance's Southern Command to a European officer instead of an American.
France has insisted that the Southern Command be set aside for a European as a pre-condition for its re-integration.

"France is not alone on this issue. The idea of a European defence identity is a European position, and France and Spain are on the same wave-length on this matter," French Foreign Ministry spokesman Yves Doutriaux said.
"France's position is well known," he told Reuters.
The United States has ruled out such an appointment, noting that NATO's chief asset in the region was the U.S. Sixth Fleet.

"We want our Sixth Fleet (based in Italy) under command of an American. It's a very important issue for us. I don't see any room for compromise," U.S. State Department spokesman Nicholas Burns said on Wednesday.
U.S. officials, however, have played down any differences with France, suggesting that Washington was open to a greater role for Europeans lower down in the command structure.
Spain joined NATO in 1982 under former Socialist prime minister Felipe Gonzalez, but froze integration into the military wing pending a referendum on continued membership.

The referendum, held in 1986, passed with a 52 percent majority but Gonzalez vowed Spain would stay outside NATO's military command structure and remain free of nuclear weapons, the latter a condition attached to Thursday's resolution.

Aznar, who took office in May after 13 years of Socialist rule, says an alliance decision this year to allow European allies to use NATO equipment and resources for their own operations boosted support for Spain's full integration.
"Since 1990, the Atlantic alliance has experienced a profound process of transformation to adapt its political and military structures to the new geo-strategic environment," the resolution said.
Parliament's backing empowers the government to negotiate Spain's position in the 16-member alliance.
In those negotiations, Spain will demand a sub-regional NATO command on its soil controlling all of the Iberian peninsula and access to the Mediterranean through the Straits of Gibraltar.
Serra said he expects talks with NATO to be completed by spring at which time Spain's integration will be finalised.
